problem_text: Show that if an ideal I in a Noetherian ring R can be generated by a regular sequence, then it can be generated by a set of elements that is a regular sequence in any order.
solution_text: Set rs' = rs. By the permutation invariance theorem for regular sequences in Noetherian rings, any permutation of a regular sequence is again a regular sequence. The proof proceeds by: (1) reducing to the case of adjacent transpositions (swapping two consecutive elements), (2) proving the two-element case: if (x, y) is a regular sequence with (x,y) proper, then (y, x) is also regular — this uses the fact that y is a non-zerodivisor on R via a Krull intersection argument (if ya=0 then a∈(x), write a=bx, then yb=0 so b∈(x), giving a∈∩(x^n)=0 by Noetherianity), and (3) noting that adjacent transpositions generate the full symmetric group, so any permutation preserves regularity.
solution_summary: rs' = rs itself works because any permutation of a regular sequence in a Noetherian ring remains regular; the proof reduces to adjacent transpositions and uses Krull's intersection theorem for the two-element case.
answer: rs' = rs suffices: any permutation of a regular sequence generating I in a Noetherian ring R is also a regular sequence generating I.
structure_features: Existence proof where the witness is the original sequence itself. The non-trivial content is proving a structural property (permutation invariance of regular sequences) that makes the trivial construction work. Reduces to adjacent transposition lemma via symmetric group generation.
knowledge_required: Symmetric group generated by adjacent transpositions
key_insight: rs' = rs itself works — the original regular sequence already has the permutation invariance property in a Noetherian ring, so the construction is trivial once the structural theorem is established.

expected_ai_method: Bare AI would try to construct a specific permutation of rs or attempt direct induction on sequence length without knowing the adjacent transposition lemma or Krull's intersection theorem.
correct_method: Set rs' = rs and prove permutation invariance: reduce to adjacent transpositions, prove the two-element case using Krull's intersection theorem and Noetherianity, then lift to all permutations via symmetric group generation.

rounds.question: Describe what 'regular sequence in any order' means structurally. What property of regular sequences in Noetherian rings would guarantee this?
rounds.expected_answer: A regular sequence x₁,...,xₙ means each xᵢ is a non-zerodivisor on R/(x₁,...,xᵢ₋₁). 'In any order' means any permutation of the sequence is still regular. This would follow from a permutation invariance theorem for regular sequences in Noetherian rings.

rounds.expected_answer: Properties include: depth characterization, Koszul complex exactness, grade of an ideal, permutation invariance. The permutation invariance theorem states that in a Noetherian ring, any permutation of a regular sequence is again regular.

rounds.expected_answer: By Krull's intersection theorem in a Noetherian ring, ∩(xⁿ) = 0 when x is a non-zerodivisor (or more generally when (x,y) is a proper ideal). Therefore a=0, proving y is NZD on R. Similarly, x is NZD on R/(y) follows from the symmetric argument.

rounds.question: Adjacent transpositions generate the symmetric group. Therefore any permutation is a composition of adjacent transpositions, each preserving regularity.
rounds.expected_answer: Since any permutation can be written as a product of adjacent transpositions, and each adjacent transposition preserves regularity (by the two-element lemma applied within the appropriate quotient ring), any permutation of a regular sequence is regular.
